There is an hour between three and four in the morning that does not seem to belong to any day of the week. Tuesday has already packed its things and left; Wednesday has not yet arrived to take custody. It is a narrow corridor of time carpeted in streetlight glare and distant highway static. If you find yourself awake in it—not because you stayed out too late, and not because you have a flight to catch, but simply because your eyes opened in the dark and refused to close again—the best thing you can do is stop wrestling the pillow, put on a coat, and step outside.

At that hour, a city looks like a theater set after the audience has gone home and the crew has left the ghost light burning. The parked cars sit nose to tail like sleeping cattle. A traffic signal at an empty intersection cycles patiently from green to amber to red, governing nobody, loyal to an unseen schedule. There is something oddly moving about that loyalty. In the daytime, everything feels personal and frantic, aimed squarely at your nerves. At three in the morning, the machinery hums on without asking anything of you.

Walk a few blocks and you realize the world never actually shuts down; it simply changes shifts. Down on Mercer Street, the sidewalk vents of the corner bakery exhale a sudden, heavy plume of yeast and cardamom, fogging the cold air. Someone is down in that basement already, forearms dusted with flour, sliding sheet pans into iron heat so that strangers will have something warm to tear apart beside their commuter coffee four hours from now. Two avenues over, a municipal sweeper creeps along the curb, its rotating bristles whispering against the asphalt as it swallows bottle caps, cigarette butts, and the last brittle leaves of autumn.

I usually drift toward the twenty-four-hour laundromat on Fourth, if only to stand near the plate glass for a minute and borrow its warmth. Fluorescent tubes buzz overhead, painting the linoleum a clean, forgiving white. Inside, a woman in a quilted vest sits on a bolted-down plastic chair, watching a giant front-loading drum churn a tangle of blue bedsheets. Beside her rests a dented thermos and a paperback whose spine has been cracked so many times the cover curls upward like bark. She does not look lonely. She looks unbothered, which is a different thing altogether. During waking hours, nearly everyone wears a thin glaze of performance—checking watches, rehearsing answers, arranging their faces for the casual surveillance of sidewalks. At three-thirty in the morning, the audition is over. You are allowed to just sit and watch the soapy water spin.

People speak of insomnia as a kind of exile, a punishment handed down by a restless mind. And sometimes it is. Left alone in a bedroom, the dark magnifies every unpaid bill, every clumsy sentence you spoke seven years ago, every fragile thing you love that could break tomorrow. An anxious mind loves a quiet room; it will haul every crate down from the attic and empty the contents across your floor.

Out on the pavement, though, the scale shifts. Private worries shrink to their proper size when placed beside the steady competence of the night. Up on the fifth floor of the brick apartment building across the street, a single kitchen window glows yellow. Maybe a new parent is pacing there with a wakeful infant, murmuring nonsense into a tiny ear while rocking from heel to toe. Maybe an old man is slicing an apple because his knees ache too much to lie flat. Maybe someone is writing a letter they will fold in half and never mail. We imagine ourselves stranded alone in the dark, yet the night is stitched together by these small, luminous squares—a quiet archipelago of the awake.

Stay out long enough and you begin to feel the planet tilt. You cannot see it yet. The sky overhead is still the color of wet slate, and the streetlights have not blinked off. You feel it instead in your lungs: a slight sharpening of the breeze, a drop of two degrees just before the sun starts prying at the eastern horizon. A delivery van rattles past, its headlights sweeping the brick storefronts and briefly illuminating the dusty mannequins in a tailor’s window before returning them to shadow. Somewhere high in a sycamore, a sparrow tests a single, tentative note, pauses as if startled by its own voice, and then tries another.

That is always my cue to turn back. The hinge is swinging shut. Soon the buses will groan awake at the depot, the espresso grinders will shriek, and the first commuters will step onto their porches, pulling their collars up as they step back into their names, their calendars, and their obligations.

I climb my front stairs, ease the key into the deadbolt so it barely clicks, and slip off my shoes in the hallway. My bed is still rumpled from the restless battle I abandoned an hour ago, only now it looks generous. I lie down just as a faint blue begins to gather along the window frame, carrying with me the small, unexpected comfort of knowing that even when we close our eyes and let go of the wheel, the world keeps turning—tended faithfully by strangers in the dark.
